readingInstruction: Read 1 Kings 20:1-22:53. Ahab’s wars with Syria, the story of Naboth’s vineyard, and the death of Ahab are told here. Notice the way God uses prophets to confront the king, and the key difference between the true prophet Micaiah and the 400 who tell the king what he wants to hear.
settingTheScene: After Carmel, Ahab remains king, and the chapters that follow show him at war with Syria and in conflict with the prophets. The story of Naboth’s vineyard is one of the most disturbing accounts of abuse of power in Scripture. The section ends with an alliance between Ahab and Jehoshaphat, the godly king of Judah, and a battle at Ramoth-gilead where Ahab dies.
observation: A prophet tells Ahab that God will give him victory over the Syrians “that you may know that I am the LORD” (20:13).
The Syrians say, “The LORD is a god of the hills but he is not a god of the valleys,” and God defeats them again (20:28).
Ahab spares Ben-hadad, and a prophet says, “Your life shall be for his life” (20:34-42).
Naboth refuses to sell his vineyard: “The LORD forbid that I should give you the inheritance of my fathers” (21:3).
Jezebel arranges false witnesses and has Naboth stoned (21:5-14).
Elijah confronts Ahab: “Have you killed and also taken possession?” (21:19).
Ahab humbles himself, and God delays the disaster (21:27-29).
The prophet Micaiah says, “As the LORD lives, what the LORD says to me, that I will speak” (22:14).
interpretation:
Chapter 20 shows God’s patience with Ahab. Twice he gives him victory over a stronger enemy, so that Ahab will know that God is the LORD. The Syrians’ belief that the LORD is a god of the hills only is corrected. His power is not limited by geography. Yet Ahab fails to follow through, making a treaty with a man God had devoted to destruction.

Chapter 21 shows what power does when it ignores God. Ahab wants a vineyard. Naboth refuses on principle: it is his family’s inheritance, given under the covenant law (Leviticus 25:23). Ahab goes home to sulk. Jezebel takes over, forges letters, arranges a show trial with false witnesses, and Naboth is killed. The scene mimics a legal process while committing murder. When Ahab comes to take the vineyard, Elijah is waiting. “Have you killed and also taken possession?” This is one of the great confrontations of the Bible. A prophet stands against a king to defend the rights of a poor man.

Naboth’s story shows that God cares about justice, property, and truth. The abuse of the weak by the powerful is not outside his concern. The prophets will return to this theme in Amos and Micah, which you will read later in this unit.

The most surprising detail is that Ahab humbles himself when he hears the judgment. He tears his clothes and fasts. And God sees it, and delays the disaster to the next generation. The mercy of God is wide. Even a wicked man’s partial repentance is noticed.

In chapter 22, Ahab asks 400 prophets whether to go to battle. They all say yes. Jehoshaphat asks, “Is there not here another prophet of the LORD?” Micaiah is the one prophet who says what God says, and it is bad news. He stands alone against the crowd. The story ends with Ahab disguised in battle, struck by a random arrow, and dying as the prophets said. The word of the LORD stands.
connection: Jesus, too, stood alone before a crowd and spoke the truth. He defended the vulnerable and confronted powerful men (Matthew 23). The false witnesses at Naboth’s trial recall the false witnesses against Jesus (Matthew 26:59-61). Jesus said, “Woe to you when all people speak well of you, for so their fathers did to the false prophets” (Luke 6:26). Hebrews 11:36-38 speaks of the faithful who suffered for the truth.
application:
Ask whether you are listening to the voices that tell you what you want to hear.

Think about someone who has less power than you. Are you protecting them?

Speak the truth in love this week, even when it is costly.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that he sees the poor and hears the cry of the wronged.
Ask him for the courage of Micaiah to speak what he says.
Ask him to keep you from the chorus of flatterers.
